explanations.explanation: Long ago, baker. The song says God's wonders are “plans formed long ago.” Nothing was cooked up at the last minute here. My own plans usually get made while I'm standing in front of an open oven, so this impresses me.

Not quite, baker. The song says these are “plans formed long ago.” So nobody had to scramble on the day it happened. I've thrown a batch together in a hurry before, but the song has something much older in mind.

Close to the right idea, but the timing is off by a lot. The song says “plans formed long ago,” and that's much older than last year. The song also says God worked them out in perfect faithfulness. My recipes don't last that long, and I stamp them for a living.
Not this time, baker. The song says the opposite about the fortress of strangers: “it will never be rebuilt.” It's a city no more. No contractor is coming back for that one.
Right, it's False. The song says the fortress of strangers “is a city no more; it will never be rebuilt.” That's final. No rebuilding, no comeback tour.
That's it, baker. The song says, “Therefore, a strong people will honor You.” It goes on to say the cities of ruthless nations will revere Him. Even the strong ones end up bowing their heads.

That's not what the song says. It says a strong people will honor God, and the cities of ruthless nations will revere Him (Isaiah 25:3). Strong people hiding would be like me hiding from my own oven. That's not the picture here.
The song goes the other way, baker. It says, “Therefore, a strong people will honor You.” The cities of ruthless nations will revere Him too. Nobody in that verse is picking a fight.
Yes, baker. The song says God has been “a refuge for the poor, a stronghold for the needy in distress.” Those are the ones He covers. I think that's a good thing to know about Him.

Good guess, but that's not who the song names. It says God has been “a refuge for the poor, a stronghold for the needy in distress.” The kings and the mighty don't show up in that line. It's the folks in distress who get the shelter.

The song doesn't name them here, baker. It says God has been “a refuge for the poor, a stronghold for the needy in distress.” That's who gets the shelter in this verse. Priests and elders aren't in the line.

Right, silenced. The song says, “so the song of the ruthless is silenced.” It's like a cloud sliding over the sun and cooling everything down. Quiet comes in, and I'd take that over the noise any day.
Not quite, baker. The song says, “so the song of the ruthless is silenced.” Nobody is playing that tune twice. Even the catchy ones don't get a second round.
The song says the opposite, baker. It says the song of the ruthless “is silenced,” like a cloud's shade cooling the heat. The shouting stops. That's one less thing to hear over the oven timer.
That's right, baker. The LORD of Hosts will prepare a lavish banquet “for all the peoples.” It's a wide-open table. I like a guest list that big.
Not quite, baker. Isaiah says the LORD of Hosts will prepare a lavish banquet “for all the peoples.” That's far wider than one group. The table isn't just for priests.
Not quite, baker. The banquet is “for all the peoples,” says Isaiah. It's a big guest list, and it isn't limited to kings. Plenty of seats at this one.
Yes, death. Isaiah says, “He will swallow up death forever.” That comes right after the shroud and the sheet. It's the biggest thing on that list, and it fits.
Not the sea, baker. Isaiah says, “He will swallow up death forever.” The sea doesn't show up in that line. The thing being swallowed up is much heavier than water.
Not the night, baker. Isaiah says, “He will swallow up death forever.” Death is the one named after the shroud. The night isn't in that verse.
Not this one, baker. Isaiah says, “He will swallow up death forever.” That word is forever, not a little while. No expiration date on that.
That's right, it's False. Isaiah says, “He will swallow up death forever.” Not for a little while, forever. Nothing temporary about it.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says, “The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face.” Every face, not just a few. I think that's one of the most tender lines in this whole passage.
Not dust, baker. Isaiah says, “The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face.” Dust is on my counter all the time, but it's tears that He wipes away. And He does it for every face.

Not sweat, baker. Isaiah says, “The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face.” I stand by an oven all day, so I know sweat well. But tears are what this verse is about, and that's a much more tender thing.
Yes, baker. They say, “we have waited for Him, and He has saved us.” They say it again: “This is the LORD for whom we have waited.” Waiting is what they talk about, twice.
Close, but that's not the word. They say, “we have waited for Him, and He has saved us.” They say it twice, actually. So waiting is the word, not searching.
That's not what they say, baker. They say, “we have waited for Him, and He has saved us.” No hammers in that verse. Waiting is the whole story.
That's it, trampled. Isaiah says, “Moab will be trampled in his place.” Moab is a neighboring nation. The verse is blunt, and it's heavy.
No crown here, baker. Isaiah says, “Moab will be trampled in his place.” Moab is a neighboring nation. That's a hard line, and it's the opposite of a crown.
Not hidden, baker. Isaiah says, “Moab will be trampled in his place.” Moab is a neighboring nation. No hiding spot in this verse, and it's a heavy one.

Yes, baker. Isaiah says, “His pride will be brought low, despite the skill of his hands.” Skilled hands didn't save it. I've got a mustache that handles a whole cookie box, and I still try to stay humble about it.
Not his harvest, baker. Isaiah says, “His pride will be brought low, despite the skill of his hands.” Pride is the thing that goes down. Great skill doesn't change that.
Not a temple, baker. Isaiah says, “His pride will be brought low, despite the skill of his hands.” The verse is about pride, not a building. Skill doesn't help him here.
That's right, baker. Isaiah says, “The high-walled fortress will be brought down, cast to the ground, into the dust.” Tall walls, and they end up in the dust. That's about as far down as it goes.
Not the sea, baker. Isaiah says the high-walled fortress will be “cast to the ground, into the dust.” No water in that verse. It ends up in the dust, flat on the ground.
No fire in this verse, baker. Isaiah says the high-walled fortress will be “cast to the ground, into the dust.” It comes down from high walls to the dust. That's quite a drop.
